sections.title: Where the work comes from
sections.question: Where does work come from, and does it come to him personally?
sections.ownerQuestion: Where does your work come from, and does it come to you personally?

baseline.statement: You told us your client base is steady. What keeps it steady is usually a handful of relationships and habits only you can name.

sections.title: How work is priced and quoted
sections.question: Could someone else reach his number?
sections.ownerQuestion: Could someone else price a job and reach your number?

baseline.statement: How you decide what to charge is almost certainly yours alone — it usually is, and nothing you told us suggests otherwise.

sections.title: How the work actually gets done
sections.question: Does the work happen without him on site?
sections.ownerQuestion: Does the work happen when you are not on site?

baseline.statement: You told us how the work actually gets done is in your head, not written down.

sections.title: Money in, money out and terms
sections.question: Who chases, who approves, what are the terms — and are supplier terms personal to him?
sections.ownerQuestion: Who chases, who approves, and are any of your supplier terms personal to you?

baseline.statement: You told us roughly $4,200,000 through the door and about $620,000 of that as owner earnings. The statements behind those sit with your accountant; what a buyer needs is the story linking them.

sections.title: Who buys, and who owns the relationship
sections.question: Revenue by customer over three years, concentration, and who owns each relationship.
sections.ownerQuestion: Who buys from you, what do they buy, and who owns each relationship?

baseline.statement: Your revenue leans on a handful of key clients and some of it is contracted or repeat. Who holds those relationships is the part a buyer asks about first.

sections.title: Who does the work
sections.question: Who is actually critical, tenure, contracts and restraints, who leaves on announcement.
sections.ownerQuestion: Who is critical, how long have they been with you, and who would leave on announcement?

sections.title: What the business owns
sections.question: Owned vs leased vs personally held; deferred maintenance; whether the premises lease transfers.
sections.ownerQuestion: What do you own, what do you lease, and what is held in your own name?

baseline.statement: You told us about $480,000 of equipment, vehicles and stock. The register and the finance paperwork are usually at the accountant's or in a drawer.

sections.title: Licences, insurance and the calendar
sections.question: The obligations calendar and who watches it; change-of-control clauses; anything in dispute.
sections.ownerQuestion: What must not lapse, and who is watching it?

sections.title: Systems & records
sections.question: Where records live, who has access, what is documented, and whether the IP is owned by the entity.
sections.ownerQuestion: Where do your records live, who can reach them, and what is written down?

baseline.statement: Which tools the business actually depends on — and who holds the logins — is not something you have told us yet.

unsorted.content: Staff details: Gary is leading hand, 24 years with the business, only other person who can price jobs, age 61. Sharon handles invoicing, payroll, and ATO work part-time (3 days/week), sister-in-law. Dylan is a fourth-year apprentice and preferred to keep. Only Gary knows mine site loading details. Nobody knows about the owner's intention to sell.

Pricing model: Service work charged at $118/hr plus materials at cost plus 22%. Tendered jobs have labour and materials plus 18% margin, except mine sites have 28% margin due to standdowns and inductions. Builders with long-term relationships on straightforward jobs get a 12% margin. Mental calculation based on drawings, not documented.

Pricing approach: Service work is charged at $118 per hour plus materials at cost plus 22%. Tendered jobs: Labour and materials computed then add 18% margin, except for mine sites where margin is 28% due to standdowns and inductions. For builders with long-term relationships and straightforward jobs, margin is reduced to 12%. This pricing is not documented and is mentally calculated based on drawings.

What he said he wants to work on, in his own words when he set me up: I run a commercial electrical and mechanical contracting business I started 35 years ago. I am starting to think about selling in the next two to five years and almost nobody knows. I want to get what is in my head written down so the business is worth something without me.

Your own valuation, from the thirteen questions you answered before signing up (Electrical & Mechanical Contracting): worth today $1,700,000, worth once your knowledge is captured $1,970,000, so the gap is $271,000.
